definitions.explanation: A vivid red-orange color traditionally derived from cinnabar (mercury sulfide), associated with shrines and traditional art.

examples.japanese: {朱|しゅ}に{染|そ}まった{鳥居|とりい}。
examples.english: A torii gate painted in vermillion.

examples.japanese: {朱|しゅ}の{色|いろ}が{鮮|あざ}やかだ。
{先生|せんせい}が{朱|しゅ}で{答案|とうあん}を{添削|てんさく}した。
examples.english: The teacher corrected the exam paper in red ink.

examples.japanese: {漆器|しっき}に{朱|しゅ}を{塗|ぬ}って{仕上|しあ}げる。
examples.english: Finish the lacquerware by applying vermillion.

notes:
A vivid red-orange color that has deep cultural significance in Japan. Originally referred to cinnabar, the mineral pigment used to produce the color.

COMMON COLLOCATIONS:
- {朱|しゅ}に{染|そ}まる: be dyed vermillion
- {朱色|しゅいろ}: vermillion (the color name)
- {朱|しゅ}{塗|ぬ}り: vermillion-lacquered
- {朱|しゅ}を{入|い}れる: add corrections in red; also, to make corrections or revisions
- {朱肉|しゅにく}: red ink pad (for stamps)

SIMILAR WORDS:
- {赤|あか}: red — the general word for red; {朱|しゅ} is more orange-tinged and culturally specific
- {紅|べに}/{紅|くれない}: crimson, deep red — a cooler, bluer red than {朱|しゅ}
- {丹|に}: red earth pigment — an older, more literary word for red pigment

CULTURAL NOTE:
Vermillion is the iconic color of Shinto {鳥居|とりい} gates and many shrine buildings. It was believed to ward off evil spirits. The expression {朱|しゅ}に{交|まじ}われば{赤|あか}くなる ("if you mix with vermillion, you turn red") is a proverb meaning you are influenced by the company you keep.
